Before reading the letter, I may say that I communicated with the writer, and the first thing I did was to ask him whether he had taken part in the rioting, because I say at once that I would not want to bring before the House the case of a man who was one of the rioters. This is what this man says:
In answer to your letter requesting details of the wounds which I received during the time of -the Quebec riots, and asking me whether I was one of the rioters, I may state that I was not. I was travelling on St. Valier street when I was attacked. I was going home at half past five in the afternoon on Sunday the 31st of March, the day before the riots. I was bayoneted four times. These bayonets penetrated the abdomen and moreover I was struck by the butt end of a rifle on the head to such an extent that my health has diminished fifty per cent and according to my physicians I will be obliged to undergo an operation every two years for the rest of my life. I have given full information to Doctors George Racine and Simard, of the Hotel Dieu, and if I should happen to forget anything, these people will give you the details.
There was more than that. We find that the prejudice became so pronounced that when men, wounded and perhaps on the point of dying, called for priests so that they might receive the last rites of the Church, even the priests were grossly insulted by the soldiers. An investigation was held subsequently, as you know, Sir, and from this information I have gathered the following evidence. This is the evidence that was given by Father Evain, a priest from France, an Oblate Father of the Parish of St. Sauveur, Quebec.
I was called upon about 10.45 on the evening of April 1 to give the last rites of the church to some of the wounded.
When I first heard the sound of firing I was in my own room and on looking through the window I saw a crowd at the corner of St. Valier and Sauvageau streets. I saw young men running along Sauvageau. I noticed a group of thirty or forty young men and heard at the same time a burst of rapid fire. Some one called out to me, "Father, you will be killed," to which I answered, "I am a Frenchman and am not afraid." Some of the young men wished to accompany me, but I told them to go home and I continued on alone.
On Demers at the corner of Ragot I saw two men lying on the ground. One of them was wounded and I gave him the rites of the church. Almost as soon as I had finished this task 1 heard behind me reports of firearms and I saw soldiers in a kneeling position firing towards Sauvageau street. I approached them and speaking in English, said ,"For Heaven's sake, don't shoot. They are only passersby and there is no danger." A soldier told me to go to Hell.
I did not answer but looked at him sorrowfully, and he said "Get away from here." I answered, "My friend, I am here to do my duty as much as you." The soldier then told

me that in firing they were acting under orders and that they would shoot any one that would show his head. On my statement that the order was very severe, I was told "Shut your mouth."
A door opened on Demers street and the soldiers went towards it. They again got into a kneeling position ready to fire. The police constable said to them, "There is a woman in the doorway." The answer was, "She has no business to come out."
The witness adds that at the time he left his presbytery at 11.15 business had been re-established and there were only about thirty or forty people in sight but that nevertheless two or three salvos were fired.
Many other cases have come to my knowledge, and though it may be tiresome for the House to listen, II believe it is my duty to bring them before Parliament and the country. The next is the case of young George Demeules, fourteen years of age. His mother, Madam Leumena Berube, appeared as a witness at the coroner's inquest and gave evidence as follows:
The deceased and his brother had procured for themselves tickets for a euchre which was to be held in the hall of the Garde Champlain. They left the house at about 8.30. The other boy Albert, aged 16 years, who had started for the euchre returned about 11.16 stating that there had been no entertainment owing to the small number of people in the hall.
A short time afterwards I was told that one of my children had been wounded in the knee. I went to the home of Depure, Sauvageau street, where I found my child lying dead.
This woman has written me the following letter:
St. Malo, March 17, 1920.
Mr. Geo. Parent,
Sir,-I read in a newspaper an article relating to the claims of the innocent victims of the riots of 1918.
I am the mother of young George Demeules, age 14 years and ten months, who was killed on the first of April, 1918. I am a poor widow and have to support a family of ten children. By the death of my son George I lost one of the main supports of the family.
Would you be kind enough, Sir, to help me in my affliction.
The next is the case of Mr. J. Alfred Mercier, a civil employee in the Crown Lands Department of the Quebec Government. He is past fifty and is known to many citizens of Quebec as one of the most peaceable men you could meet. He describes in the following letter what happened :
I was coming from St. Roch going in the direction of St. Sauveur, when at a place called Boulevard Langelier, I saw a few soldiers who appeared to be on the watch; everything seemed to me perfectly quiet, and there were no civilians at that particular place. A soldier came to meet me, and I asked him if I

could cross on the other side of the street to reach ray home- Seeing that these men were English-speaking, I put this question to him in his own language. He said quite politely that if I wanted to go in, that direction I had to take an upper street (pointing at St.-Valier street), and go right straight ahead. X did obey at once, and taking St. Val-ier street I kept on walking. A few acres further I saw 'hut twelve soldiers standing. There also everything was quiet, and there were no civilians in sight. I was going to put to these men the same question I had just asked- when a soldier nearer to me suddenly rushed with his bayonet. I made a step backward-, raised my hands, and I made this remark in the English language: That I was not armed, that I was going to my home, and I asked him if I could pass at this place. He then answered me: "No, nobody is allowed to pass here. If you want to go that way, you have to take another street." I answered: "All right, I will take -St. Jude's street," and X turned around. I had scarcely done so when a -bullet was fired and went through my left arm about two inches below the elbow. I was then able to make a few steps further, and I went into a house from where the military ambulance came and got me to the hospital.
At that moment it was 9.30- o'clock in the evening, and the troubles which happened that night did not begin until about 11 o'clock. Therefore, there was no justification whatever to fire on a peaceful and well-behaved citizen. After prolonged sufferings it is decided that my arm will remain crooked, and the fingers and the wrist are such that I shall never be able to make use of them.
Then there is the case of Mr. Edouard Tremblay. A lawyer was consulted about his case with the view of finding out whether the city of Quebec could be held responsible for the injuries he had suffered, or whether somebody else, perhaps the Government, could be held responsible. The young lawyer who was consulted is a prominent young man of Quebec City, who has studied at Oxford University. He had won the first prizes in Quebec province which entitled him to study at the English university. This young lawyer held the view that the city of Quebec was not responsible and consequently he did not take any action against the city. He has sent me some details of this case and believes that the country should do something for his client. He has sent me the following letter in French:
Quebec, March 1-5, 1910. Mr. George Parent, M.P.,
House of Commons,
Ottawa,
Dear Mr. Parent,-I was pleased to hear that you had moved for an Order of the House asking for information concerning the innocent victims who, during the so-called Quebec riot in 1918 were killed or wounded by soldiers of His Majesty.
I represented at the coroner's inquest one of my fellow-countrymen of Murray Bay, who was one of the unfortunate victims; it was
young Edward Tremblay, then a student at the Technical school.
I now come to give you information, for I do not believe that a claim was forwarded to Ottawa in his case.
This Mr. Edward Tremblay was to complete his studies at the Technical school in June, 1918. He was a son of M.rs. Joseph Tremblay, a widow from River-Mailloux, Murray Bay, in the county of Charlevoix.
At the time of the so-called riot in Quebec, he was at home on a holiday. He came to Quebec on April 1st, the very day he was killed near Bagot street. He came by the Quebec and Saguenay, about five o'clock and during the evening, after supper he went for a walk with a cousin of his. It was while -thus walking that he was killed in the vicinity of Bagot street by a shot in the leg and another in the elbow.
The inquest positively established that neither of the wounds was deadly; according to the statement of Dr. Marois "there was no cause for his dying." In fact, if upon that occasion there had been an ambulance or somebody to give him emergency treatment, his case would not have been serious. However, having been wounded about ten o'clock, first aid was only given him about one o'clock in the morning by Dr. Marois himself. Unfortunately . he was then much exhausted and it was too late. He died in the morning of the day after, about eight o'clock.	.
I made numerous endeavours to get from the corporation of the city of Quebec some compensation in behalf of his unfortunate mother. On April 30, 191'8, I sent to His Honour the mayor and aldermen a registered letter applying for fair and reasonable compensation. They acknowledged my letter, and that was all. Then, seeing that I was of the opinion that the family was entitled to compensation on political grounds, I advised them to refrain from entering legal proceedings.
I would be grateful to you if you were willing to lay that information before the House when the question is debated. I really think this case is one of the most soul-stirring.
Thanking you in advance, I am,
Tours truly,

Briefly, the foregoing letter contains the following facts. Edward Tremblay, the son of a widow, Mrs. Joseph Tremblay, of Riviere Mailloux La Malbaie, Charlevoix, was a student who would have graduated from the technical school in June, 1918. He arrived in Quebec on the first of April at about four p.m., and during the course of the evening was found dead as the result of a bullet wound in the leg and the elbow, the shooting having taken place in Bagot street. The investigation showed positively that neither of his wounds was mortal, and in the opinion of Dr. Marois the man's life could have been saved. Indeed, had an ambulance been on the spot, and had first aid been given this young man his case would not have -been even serious. He was wounded about ten o'clock in the evening ibut was not attended to in any way until about one o'clock the following -morn-

ing, when it was too late to hope for his recovery. Owing to extreme weakness from loss of Iblood he died. The lawyer to whom I have referred thinks that this case is one of the saddest in his experience, and I think myself that the facts bear out this opinion. Another unfortunate case has been brought to my notice, and it is to my mind more serious than the other. If the former case appeals to the sympathy of the Government, the exceedingly sad circumstances which I am about to narrate will, I am sure, .meet with a still greater degree of sympathy and regret. I refer to the case of Avila Bloin, which was taken up by a lawyer of Quebec named Armand Lavergne, who instituted before the courts an action for damages against the city, on his behalf, for the sum of $140,000. Judgment has been rendered, the court dismissing the action on the ground that any responsibility in the matter must lie, not with the city of Quebec but rather with the country at large, or, in other words, with the Government. Now, Mr. Speaker, here is a young man well educated, steady, and reliable who begins his career in life as the proprietor of a garage, attending to most of the work himself, and whose prospects in life have been very materially impaired as a result of the suffering which he has endured through no fault nor negligence of his own. I asked him to put in writing all the facts in connection with his case, and I shall give to the House a translation of his statement:
Rue Chevriere,
Parish of the Sacred Heart,
Quebec, P.Q.
Sir,-I wish to interest you in my case, which I am sure deserves special attention. I was unfortunate enough to be wounded on April 1st during the Quebec riots. I was hit in the right leg, and after two operations, I am obliged to walk with crutches since the leg has been amputated two inches below the knee. I declare upon my honour that the following is the true story of the events which occurred on the above-mentioned date.
On the night of April 1st, after having worked all evening at my garage at the corner of Des-glacis and D'Aguillon streets; this spot is quite remote from the scene of the riots.
I started for home about 11.40 p.m. On arriving at the Boulevard Tanglier I was ordered by two sentries to keep straight on. I had gone but a few steps when I heard a whistle, and I threw up my hands, thinking this to be the most prudent thing to do, since I understood no English. I retraced my steps, in order to make myself understood by the sentries who had just let me pass. Whilst I was in the act of turning I was fired upon and hit in the left leg. The leg was badly injured, and the soldiers wishing to prevent me from getting up, I presume, tied me to a post, in order to bandage my wound. I am under the impression that

they were not quite sane, because, instead of relieving my pain, they hit me on the head and in the face. Soon afterwards they carried me into a private house, and the military doctor gave orders for the ambulance to carry me to the Military Hospital. They amputated my leg without asking my consent or that of my parents, in spite of the fact that I had given them the telephone number of my home. 1 underwent treatment at the hospital for five months.
My leg was amputated twice, and I consider myself disabled to the extent of fifty per cent. It is now impossible for me to run a garage, and X have lost all hopes of the future. My incapacity X ascribe to the fact that the operation in question was so badly performed that specialists have advised me that I will find considerable difficulty in wearing an artificial limb.
I wish to call your attention to the fact that it would appear from the coroner's inquest that the officer commanding gave orders not to shoot after eleven o'clock. I was fired upon, a few minutes before midnight. I was alone, and if they had any reason to suspect me they might have taken me prisoner, and there was no necessity for shooting.
Tours very sincerely.
I may say, Mr. Speaker, that I asked this young man to state his case in writing because his interview with me was so painful, from the palpable suffering which he was enduring, that I could not prolong it. I can assure you that the experience is trying, to say the very least, to hear a man in the prime of life, well started in a prosperous business, relating a story of cruel torment, and when I could listen to his verbal statement no longer I requested him to present the facts in writing, assuring him that I should be pleased to bring them to the attention of the Government. I feel confident that if the hon. leader of the Government, the Minister of Justice, and other gentlemen on the other side of the House, could witness for themselves the sad plight of this young man, and hear from his own lips the pathetic story which he told me, they would have for him the same compassionate feeling as I had. I am sure that if they had seen him in person and heard his story they could not fail to regard it as a matter of strict justice that a man who has suffered altogether unnecessarily, and who has been deprived of his capacity to fulfil his career, deserves to be indemnified to an adequate extent.
Other cases are just as important and entitled to the same sympathy. I find that at the coroner's inquest the case of Alex. Bussieres was also presented. From the evidence of his wife, Regina Ferland, aged 22 years, it appears that upon the evening of April 1, the husband, aged 25 years, returned from work about 6.30 and asked his wife's permission to go to a pub-

lie meeting to be 'held by Mr. Armand La-vergne on Jacques Cartier Square. It was on Friday morning that she learned that her husband had been killed and that his body was at the morgue. Here was a man killed on Monday, April 1, and only on Friday morning did his wife hear that her husband is dead. She states positively that this man had in his possession a certain amount of money and a watch when he left home and that this property was never afterwards recovered or found. She also says under oath that her husband never carried weapons of any kind and that he never had any at the house.
Another case is that of F. X. Bourget. He was a worker in a shoe factory, and in his own evidence he says that he was engaged making shoes for soldiers. This is the way he was handled by them: He was walking along a certain street to go home when the soldiers fold him to turn around and go home by another route. If he did there would be some other soldiers stationed on that route who would order him 3 p.m. to turn around and go by the route along which he started first. He was about to obey the order, but the soldiers fired upon him and a bullet went through his jaw. He was transferred to the Hotel Dieu hospital, was five weeks without being able to woTk, and as a result of his injuries his earning capacity has been very much reduced.
Another case is that of George Boyte. This illustrates one of those cases which are quite [numerous in the province of Quebec, where young men begin working early in life because of the large families in that particular part of the country. They do as their fathers did. George Boyte is the son of one of the most industrious workers you can find anywhere. On that particular night, as was the custom of most of these young men, he went out to enjoy a game of pool or billiards. He had gone to a hall, had .spent the evening there and on his way home was fired upon. This is the information that I have to communicate to the House concerning him:	He was
seventeen years of age at the time of the riots. He was wounded about 10 p.m on April 1, 1918, at the corner of St. Valier and Laviolette streets. He had spent some time during the course of the evening at the Frontenac Hall, St. Roch. Because a number of soldiers were patrolling St. Joseph street, he was obliged to return home by way of St. Francis street, and whilst going through the crowd he was hit
by a rifle bullet in the elbow, with the result that his right arm is now useless owing to paralysis of the fingers. He is the oldest son of a laTge family, he has been disabled forever, and he should be entitled to some sympathy.
I referred a minute or two ago to 'the coroner's inquest. I may say that this inquest was held on the body of Honore Bergeron. I have, from the report of the coroner's inquest, the following concerning this man: His widow identified the body of her late husband, a carpenter, aged 44 years. She states:
On Monday, the day of the riot, my husband returned from work about six o'clock and had supper at home. He left after supper to go for his tool case. He returned about 9.30, when he told me that things were going badly on the boulevard. He went out shortly afterwards to look for the children, telling me that he would return shortly. During the course of the evening I heard that he had been arrested by the militia. On Tuesday and Wednesday I searched1 for him, and it was only on Thursday afternoon that I was asked to go to the morgue where I identified the corpse of my husband.
Madame Bergeron is the mother of six children, the eldest of whom is 19 years and the youngest ten months. Concerning this particular case, I had occasion, on a recent visit to the city of Quebec, to meet Dr. Leclerc, a physician of high standing, who told me that he had seen this occurrence, and he stated to me in plain language that Bergeron was at least 200 feet from the crowd when the bullet killed Mm. No doubt if further investigation takes place, we may obtain details which may lead the Government to help this widow by way of an indemnity.
The coroner's inquest was held on the body of this man and the verdict that was found was stated by the jury to be applicable to all the other cases. It is important and necessary that the country should know what the finding of the men who investigated this case was. For the information of the House and the country I may say that the Government was represented at that particular inquest by Major Gregor Barclay, an advocate of Montreal. The following is a statement of the findings of the jury with reference to the death of Ber geron, and this verdict applies to all the other cases:
Bergeron met his death at the comer of St. Valier, St. Joseph and Bagot streets on the night of Monday, April 1, 1918. He was killed toy a rifle bullet fired by the soldiers of His Majesty who were then on duty for the purpose of suppressing a riot.

The jury is of the opinion that inasmuch as the persons killed on this occasion were innocent of all participation in, this riot, which was occasioned by the 'brutal and, tactless fashion in which the federal officers charged with the execution of the conscription law carried their instructions into effect, it will be the duty of the Government to indemnify in a reasonable fashion the families of the victims who were proved to be innocent and unarmed at that time, as well as to indemnify those who suffered, loss through this riot.
The jury expressed their profound regret that the good reputation of the peaceful and law-abiding citizens of St. Roeh and St. Sauveur has been placed in jeopardy by the thoughtless act of some young men and .of some evil inten-tioned men, probably strangers to this city, who endeavoured to make capital out of this trouble.
Among the members of the jury I find the following names: J. A. Lesage, alderman; Ed. Picthe, accountant; John Laroche, druggist; F. H. Levasseur, merchant; Nazaire, Fortier, manufacturer and bank director; J. G. Scott, who is the promoter and for a long time general manager of the Quebec and Lake St. John Railway; and Martin Monaghan, insurance agent.
If this is not enough, Mr. Speaker, to justify the Government giving these cases sympathetic consideration, I might perhaps remind them that in that period of our history between 1840 and 1850 they will find a precedent for granting indemnification- and the period between 1849 and 1918 is not a very long time in the life of a nation -subsequent to the Rebellion of 1837, the Government of that day thought fit to grant compensation to the people who suffered during that disturbance. We remember well what happened then. It took a few years before the Government could be persuaded to deal with the matter, but in 1849 it was decided that compensation should be granted, and among the most prominent men who supported this course we are proud to find the name of William Lyon Mackenzie, who, I believe was the grandfather of the present leader of His Majesty's Loyal Opposition.
Undoubtedly there were difficulties in the way, and rather than attempt to present the case in my own words I had better let the historian relate what happened. I find that the question of rebellion losses, even for the rebels, had been the subject-matter of discussion for some time previous to 1849. Prior to 1841 the special Council of Lower Canada had passed an Ordinance, and the legislature of Upper Canada an Act, providing for compensation to the loyalists whose property had been destroyed by rebels.
In the first session of the Parliament of the United Provinces an Act was passed [Mr. Parent. 1
in amendment of the Upper Canada Act, including among those entitled to compensation people whose property had been wantonly or unnecessarily destroyed by the servants of the Crown, and on the 28th of February, 1845, an address was carried in the House of Assembly praying:
That His Excellency will be pleased to cause proper measures to be adopted in order to insure to the inhabitants of that part of this province, formerly Lower Canada, indemnity for just losses by them sustained during the rebellion of 1837-8.
To conform to this request a commission was appointed by Mr. Draper's Administration with instructions to discriminate between those who had taken up arms against the Crown and loyal subjects of His Majesty. On the 18th of April, 1846, the commission reported claims from 2,196 persons representing £241,965,105, and advised that £100,000 should cover the damages. No action was taken by the Government on that report.
Parliament was dissolved on the 6th of December, and a new Parliament assembled on the 25th of February. In the first session of 1848 nothing was done, but in the second session which opened on January 18, 1849, Mr. Lafontaine,-who had just been returned to power-brought in a Bill for the indemnification of persons whose property had been destroyed during the rebellion of 1837-8. This is the famous Re-hellion Losses Act of 12 Victoria, chapter 58. Lafontaine had made it plain that refusal to support some measure of compensation would probably break up the ministry which had been the choice of the people. This compensation to French Canadians, many- of whom had been actively or passively in revolt against England, roused afresh the old loyalty cry and social prejudices. Concessions to the French were regarded by the Tories as a kind of treason on a question which had been approved not only by the British members of Lower Canada but even by those in Upper Canada. The Bill passed on March 9, 1849, by a majority of 47 to 18.
I do not want to recall, Mr. Speaker, the terrible events which followed the passing of this Bill,-that those loyalists who did. not approve of the measure thought the best way to protect against it was to burn the Parliament buildings in Montreal. At the time Lord Elgin was subjected to such indignities and there were such violent disturbances that I do not think it in the interests of the case I am presenting to recite 'them.

I am satisfied, Mr. Speaker, that if the Government are in search of a precedent they will find it in the history of the period I have referred to. I have used the mildest language I can possibly think of in presenting the claims of these people, and all I am aiming at is to get for them a just and fair indemnity for what they have suffered. Happily there is a sentiment prevailing that both races in this country should unite as they did in the past under the leadership of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and it seems to me that one of the best means towards the realization of such unity would be to indemnify the persons whose cases I have brought to the attention of the House.

Mr .Speaker, my hon.
friend from Quebec West (Mr. Parent) has presented his case with so much lability and force, his argument is so complete, that I only wish to say a word for the claim which he laid before this House. It is absolutely useless to discuss the cause of the conflict which took place in Quebec in 1918. It can be sought for in several directions, and can be judged from various points of view. Fot my part, I have always been of opinion that one of the principal causes of the trouble was the unjustifiable arrogance and conduct of certain federal government agents entrusted with the carrying out of the law. Whether that be the true cause of the trouble or not, there can be no doubt that those who were its absolutely innocent victims have a right to compensation.
The city of Quebec can in no way be held responsible, as the maintenance of order and peace within its limits had been taken from it and assumed by the military authorities. The municipal authorities of the city had ceased to have any control or responsibility. Everything was in the hands of the military authorities, and if in the performance of their duties they caused any damage, the Government is responsible for their actions. People who. had taken no part in the disorders were killed, others were wounded. Poor workmen who were coming back from their work, and who were absolutely obliged to go by these streets to reach their homes, were mortally wounded, without having done anything whatever which might render them in the slightest degree responsible for these events.
Mr. Speaker, the laws of justice should he abided by in time of war as well as in time of peace. So true is this, that when the Government or the military authorities have to take over a piece of land or private property for military purposes, they always give
therefore a fair compensation to the interested party. I maintain that a humain life is more valuable than a piece of land or a house. If, in the exercise of duties thought to be necessary for the restoration of peace, or for war purposes, the soldiers have had to take the lives of innocent men who had not voluntarily made themselves liable, the authorities and the Government are certainly obliged to pay an indemnity, a fair compensation, to those who depended upon these victims for their support. I believe that the principle need only to be stated to be recognized as sound.
The Government should inquire into each of the cases mentioned by my hon. friend from Quebec West. It is possible that some case might deserve less consideration from the Government than other, but this can only be ascertained by a serious, impartial investigation; and the persons who have been injured without having done anything .entailing the slightest responsibility, have a right to be indemnified, and the country owes it to itself-it is a debt of honour-to pay them such compensation.
After all, there were expenditures during the war-I do not wish to give expression to any criticism, for it is neither the time nor place to do so-there were, I say, expenditures which many people in this country have criticized; there were many useless expenditures. The Government, I admit, have not been able to control every thing, but there has been so much money uselessly spent, that the claims submitted by my hon. friend from Quebec West to-day, should meet the sympathy of the Government and the sympathy of all right-minded people m this country.
The hon. member for Quebec West mentioned as a precedent the compensation which was paid to the victims of the rebellion of 1837-1838. The case of the victims of the Quebec disorders is much more appealing than that of the victims of 1837-1838. In 1837-1838, many were indemnified who had themselves taken part in the rebellion, who had taken a stand against the constituted authority; and yet it was thought proper ta pay them an indemnity along with the rest. In the present instance, the victims have taken no part whatever in the rioting or disorders which took place; they were struck without their having done anything that could bring upon them the fate which they met, and I believe that, under the circumstances, this House should concur in the opinion of my hon. friend for Quebec West and declare that some compensation should be paid these people.

Mr. Speaker, the question of compensation to the innocent victims of the Quebec trouble has been so fully and fairly dealt with by my two colleagues from that city that very little remains for me to say. However, I should like to direct the attention of the House to the case of one of my constituents who was injured during these troublous times. A man named A. Quart, residing on Champlain street, Quebec, was walking along St. Valier street on Sunday, March 31, 1918, accompanied by two young ladies. On reaching the corner of Blanchet street he was struck by a rifle bullet in the right shoulder and was seriously wounded, his life being seriously despaired of for a few days. The bullet was fired from a rifle in the hands of one of His Majesty's soldiers. ' The victim suffered considerable damage, which in a lawsuit which he took against the city of Quebec, he estimated at $1,200. This lawsuit was not proceeded with, because, as the member for Quebec West (Mr. Parent) has just pointed out, a previous suit had been dismissed, on the ground, if I remember rightly, that the city of Quebec was not responsible; that as the injury had been occasioned by His Majesty's troops the Dominion of Canada should be liable for indemnification. I know this young man very well. He had a brother killed at the front in 1915; so he could not have had any evil intentions or ulterior motives in proceeding along St. Valier street. I am informed that at the time he was wounded he was at a considerable distance from the scene pf any trouble or from any troops, or any group of men who might in any conceivable way be called rioters.
In studying this matter I looked up the precedents, and naturally the first one which struck me was that of the Rebellion Losses Bill. I had intended to go into that at some length, but my hon. friend (Mr. Parent) has fully explained the purport of the Rebellion Losses Bill and has made clear to the House that in this case there is far more justice in the claim of the victims for indemnification than there could have been for the victims compensated under the Rebellion Losses Bill. At the time of the passage of the Rebellion Losses Bill the feeling of the people was running very high and it must have been extremely difficult for any Government, however well disposed, to convince its followers, particularly those from Upper Canada, that' any compensation should be paid to those whom

the people of Upper Canada almost unanimously condemned as rebels. Reading the debates of those days I came across some very curious statements, and if the House will bear with me I should like to read one or two as showing the state of feeling which existed in the country at that time and showing how very difficult it must have been to induce the people of Canada to pay any compensation. I quote from a leading article in the Montreal Gazette of February 16, 1849. The Montreal Gazette, I may say, was apparently the leading Tory paper even of that time. It states:
But if the ministry force on their resolutions, and carry them, we can tell them explicitly, that they never calculated on more baseless anticipations, if they expect that that is to end the matter. The vote of the House will be the signal for a resistance, which will end in the complete prostration of the French-Canadian race-a resistance which will be carried on so long as we remain under the British Crown, and as long after as necessary.
You will see, Sir, that at that time the resistance to payment of these claims was so great that a large portion of the inhabitants of this country was prepared to renounce allegiance to the British Crown in pieference to making payment. Although feeling ran high and the debates were somewhat acrimonious, the monotony was relieved to a certain extent by incidents such as I will cite in a moment. In the Montreal Gazette of February 23, 1849, we read of a Mr. Meyers having announced that he had received a resolution from a certain portion of Upper Canada, in which resolution a number of his supporters protested against this Bill. Then the article goes on to state:
Mr. Cameron requested permission to read another telegraphic communication from Belleville, a little different from the one just read. The hon. member then read a communication from Belleville, dated 20th Febuary, which said: " Tories met at half past twelve-Reformers present protested at one-had majority-passed two resolutions-when Orangemen rushed in with clubs and pistols, and dispersed meeting."
There is no doubt whatever that the Tories of that day were somewhat exercised over the proposition to pay any of these claims. In order to show exactly what were the claims and what was the manner of payment, I should like to read the resolutions as they passed the House on Thursday, March 1, 1849, as reported in the Gazette of March 2, 1849. There were six resolutions, only one of which, as it is the principal one, I will read:
And that the said losses so far only as they have arisen from the total or partial unjust, unnecessary or wanton destructions of the dwellings, property and effects of the said in-

habitants, and by the seizure, taking or carrying away of their property and effects, should be paid and satisfied:	Provided, that none of
the persons who have been convicted of high treason alleged to have been committed in that part of this province formerly lower Canada, since the first day of November, 1837, or who, having been charged with high treason, or other offences of a treasonable nature, and having been committed to the custody of the sheriff in the gaol of Montreal, submitted themselves to the will and pleasure of Her Majesty, and were thereupon transported to Her Majesty's island of Bermuda-shall be entitled to any indemnity for losses sustained during or after the said rebellion, or in consequence thereof.
Therefore, the ease is far stronger than that which occupies our attention at the present moment. There are other precedents also. For instance, after the rebellion of 1798 in Ireland, I read, as a matter of fact in this Montreal Gazette in looking pver a speech by Sir Alan McNab, that the people of Ireland were paid a certain indemnity. In 1853, there was passed in the British House of Commons an Act, chapter 38, to extend indemnities for malicious injury to properties in Ireland, and I understand that this Act or a modification thereof, is in force in Ireland to-day and has been frequently invoked of late. This Act, if I understand the matter aright, places on the community the burden of collecting sums to met these damages. That would not apply exactly in this case, but it recognizes the principle that public authority is responsible for damages caused by a riot.
There is another incident in the history of England, although I do not know that it applies very much to this case. If my recollection is good, in the fifties, a famous debate arose in Parliament with reference to a Don Pacifico, a Portuguese Jew who had been injured in some riots, I think, in Greece. He had lost a certain quantity of furniture, chairs, clothing, etc. His case was brought before the British House of Commons, and Lord Palmerston, who was at that time Prime Minister, considered it so important that he devoted to it a speech of five hours in length. This is the famous speech which he wound up by saying " Civis Britannicus sum," and in which he threatened Greece, or whatever state it was, with the might and Majesty of the British Empire unless this Portuguese was paid every cent of damages which he had suffered. I understand that, in spite of the fact that the claims were unjust, and also, that it was shown that hardly any compensation could be justified, the British House of Commons almost unanimously declared that, in cases of this kind, in cases of riot, public authority should be made 78
to pay for damages suffered by private citizens. Therefore, the same precedent should apply to those who have suffered damages in Quebec, and all the more because I think it can be conclusively shown that at least a large number of those who were injured during the riots in Quebec were innocent spectators and were in no way connected with the rioters. At any rate it seems to me that it is the duty of the Militia Department the Department of Justice and the Government to make a full and complete investigation into every one of the cases cited by the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Parent) and other casks which I have no doubt exist and which would doubtless be brought to the attention of any investigating body.

speakeroldname: Rt. Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there can, of course, be and there is no objection whatever to this motion being adopted and the papers being brought down. Having said that, I have, perhaps, said as much as can be expected from me with regard to this motion.
I will, however, permit myself to call the attention of the hon. gentleman to the fact that it does not appear from his recital of the different cases which he enumerated that the circumstances of those cases were brought to the attention of the department that would be concerned-in this case the Department of Militia and Defence- by any otheT method than the present motion. I am not affirming that it is not so, but I do not understand that his case rests on the facts that it was.
Upon a motion of this kind it must be obvious to the House that it is quite impossible that anybody should come here prepared to make answer with regard to the circumstances of the particular oases cited. 1 do not fancy that even the hon. gentleman himself expected that anybody here would be in a position to deal with those cases. The motion itself, of course, makes no reference to any particular case or cases, and so far as I am aware the hon. gentleman did not intimate in any way to the Government, and certainly not to me, what particular cases, if any, he intended to refer to. I fancy I am correct in saying that no such intimation was given to the Minister of Militia. I do not say this for the purpose of criticizing. I am not saying that the hon. gentleman was not within his right; I say it only for the purpose of making it perfectly cleai; that it is not possible in the nature of things for any one speaking on behalf of such department of the Government as may be particularly concerned or



on behalf of the Government itself, to make any answer as to the accuracy of the iiircum-stances as recited of the particular cases dealt with.
It is also to be pointed out that if the impression remaining with me after my careful following of the address of the hon. gentle man is correct, that he rests his case upon the ex parte statements either of the individuals who claim to have been affected or of those interested in enforcing a claim- and I am not suggesting that these people are necessarily not telling the truth. I think the hon. gentleman himself will agree with me that it would not be proper for this Government to determine to take action and disburse the moneys of the people of this country simply upon the basis of the statements that have been read to this House without opportunity for verification in any way. It is perhaps a little surprising, if those cases be really well founded, that those interested should have waited three years and should then address letters to members of Parliament and seek to bring about a remedy by submitting their claims to Parliament, which itself directly can bring no remedy to hear. As I have said, there is no objection to bringing down all the papers that bear upon the unfortunate incidents that occurred in the city of Quebec at the time referred to.
As to what I understand to be the general principle implied, at all events in the observations of the hon. gentleman who made the motion, and affirmed and put perhaps more distinctly by the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe), supported by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), I think no one will be surprised when I say that-with this motion upon the Order Paper one would not come here expecting to take up and discuss, still less to determine, the soundness or unsoundness of this proposition. I want to concede that it was put forward, if I may be permitted to say so, in what seemed to me very suitable and very moderate language, and I am not prepared to say at the present moment that that proposition is not one calling for consideration or to say the very least, a proposition in whose support possibly much that is well founded may he said. With regard to that proposition I can at the present moment only say-and I fancy that the strongest supporter of the motion would expect no more of me under present circumstances-that I shall certainly be glad to give consideration to it, and to approach it with a desire simply to look into the justification or lack of justi-
fication that may be found for it. Of course as to whether the general proposition should be accepted as being sound-that general proposition being, as I understand it, that, if you assume on the one hand that the action of the Government was not subject to criticism but was a necessary action in the general interest, and on the other hand, that the particular persons injured were perfectly innocent persons, under those circumstances it would be proper to assimilate the injury done to those persons to the damage suffered by individuals -whose properties are taken in the general interest, and that therefore proper compensation for those injuries would be justified as being an indemnification to a party suffering by some perfectly proper action necessarily taken in -the public interest-I did not, of course, come here expecting to be asked to pass a final opinion upon a question of that kind, and I can say nothing more except that I shall be glad to give consideration, and to ask my colleagues to give consideration, to the proposition that has been put forward, and to weigh carefully what has in support of that proposition been so moderately and at the same time so clearly put forward. The papers will be brought down.
Mr. HENRI E, LAVIGUEUR (Quebec) (translation) :	Mr. Speaker, Although I
have not listened to the whole discussion just carried on, I would beg leave to make a few observations upon this important question.
In the first place I should say that I have been pleased to hear the right hon. the Minister of Justice declare that he will take the matter under consideration and that, if possible, the unfortunate victims of the disorders of two years ago in Quebec, or their relatives will be compensated. Without, any intention of censuring or finding fault in any way whatsoever as to the action then taken by the Militia Department, I believe that the deplorable incidents alluded to would probably never have come to pass in Quebec, had a little more prudence and, especially, a little more moderation been shown. Had the Government buildings been protected in the way we had suggested; had the registrar's office -in the Auditorium building-been protected according to our recommendations, when it was reported that a riot had been started, and that the registrar's office would likely be its principal object; had, in short, the appeal then made by the mayor and the municipal authorities of Quebec, been heed-

ed, I think such incidents -would not have taken place or, at any event, not on so large a scale.	*
I believe it would be absolutely proper, under the circumstances, for the Government to indemnify the victims of this unfortunate affair who have suffered so greatly, and especially the innocent victims, peaceful people who were wounded without any provocation whatever.
Motion agreed to.

Mr. H. H. STEVENS (Vancouver Centre) "moved:
That, in the opinion of this House, it is expedient to amend the Water Carriage of Goods Act, chapter sixty-one of the Statutes of 1910, by providing that the said Act shall also apply to ships carrying goods from any port outside of Canada to any port in Canada, and to goods carried by such ships or received to be carried by such ships.
He said: I should not take up the time of the House with this resolution were it not necessary, under the rules, to precede by resolution a Bill having reference to trade and commerce. Under the advice of Parliamentary Counsel, therefore, I was compelled to put this resolution on the Order Paper. I may remark that this resolution was on the Order Paper last year, when it was suggested that the matter might be allowed to stand, as it was in the nature of a notice of motion, so that any interested parties might have an opportunity to prepare any views which they might desire to express on the subject. It is not my intention to argue the matter at great length, but rather to bring to the attention of the House some reasons for the resolution and the Bill which will be founded upon it. I shall ask the House, when I have completed my remarks, to permit me to introduce the Bill, and shall suggest that the Bill be referred to one of the standing committees, such as the Committee on Railways, Canals, and Telegraph Lines, in order that any one desirous to do so may have an opportunity of presenting any opinions on the subject involved. I am quite aware that this resolution deals with a matter of a controversial character, and that there are interests in Canada that may consider their rights to be infringed and may desire to be heard. I shall base the appeal for the introduction of the Bill upon certain reasons which I shall briefly state. It has been the custom of owners and charterers of ships to insert in bills of lading special clauses contracting themselves out of liability for damage to 78i
goods carried. This practice has been the cause of the complaint, if I may so term it, which shippers have advanced in connection with this matter. Shippers contend that it has not been possible for them to obtain justice in regard to claims for damaged goods carried in ships because of the forms used in bills of lading, and in a moment or two I shall give to the House a striking case in point. I understand that, according to the old common law of England, ship-owners are liable for the proper and safe delivery of goods, this liability being limited only bv certain well-understood exceptions. But the practice which I have just mentioned, of inserting special clauses in bills of lading, has largely resulted in a departure from this well-known principle. There is no bill of lading common to all countries. Every country has a different form to suit its own purposes, and I presume that it will be a good many years at least before a universal form of bill of lading will be adopted. This diversity in the use of forms also adds to the difficulty; and shippers have found that when goods have arrived in port in a damaged condition the only way by which they could have their claims properly considered was to libel the ship. Now, it is obvious that any persons or firms libelling a ship in the event of the case going against them they will pay for the time the ship may have been delayed. This of course is a very heavy responsibility, especially where the amount of the claim bears no reasonable comparison to the risk involved. This question was taken up by the Dominion Royal Commission, of which the right hon. leader of the House (Sir George Foster) was chairman. That commission submitted a report, a copy of which I have on my desk, and to which I shall briefly refer. In section 595 the report refers to this question, stating that the commissioners have looked into the matter with the utmost care, having studied the laws as they obtain in the various dominions, in the United States, and in the United Kingdom, and declares that frequently ship-owners endeavour-I shall give the exact words of the report-
To contract themselves out of liability for loss or damage in respect of the goods which they carry, particularly from the United Kingdom to the self-governing dominions-
I desire the 'House to pay particular attention to the following words:
to an extent unfair in itself.
This very important commission which travelled all over the Empire, very carefully taking exhaustive evidence on the sub-

ject, states that in its opinon the practice in question was one that was unfair, adding:
In our consideration of this question we have studied the views tendered in evidence hy shipowners, as well as hy shippers, and we have also had the opportunity of considering the discussion on the question which took place at the conference on merchant shipping legislation in 1907 between representatives of the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand.
The report goes on to say:
It is admitted also that until a comparatively recent date ship-owners generally accepted these liabilities, and did not attempt to contract themselves out of them.
At this point I may observe that responsible lines operating regularly between various ports in the world seldom try to contract themselves out of liability, hut dramp ships and small lines that do not call regularly, simply picking up cargo and carrying it here and there as opportunity offers, frequently take advantage of the special contracts superimposed upon their bills of lading, and thus cause a loss to shippers.
How could we exercise control over, tramp ships by any law we might enact?
That is exactly what this Bill proposes to do.
What would be the use of passing a Bill if we could not enforce it?
Could they not have libelled the ship and put up a bond? Would that not have protected the owners of the ship?

They could have libelled the ship; that is quite right but the owners would not consent to the bond. They said: No, you can libel our ship and we will wait till the case is tried but you must incur all the risk of demurrage. That is exactly the method employed by the owners of such vessels. They know that the average person will not libel a ship and incur the risk. Virtually there is no reasonable possibility of a shipper securing any-redress under the present law.
Now, it -may be claimed, and is claimed by many, that if we pass this amendment there will be a tendency to drive shipping away from our ports. I have under my hand a statement that several large importers in the United States who desired to foring shipments through Vancouver- and the same thing will apply to the eastern ports-refrained from doing so simply because they found they had no protection such -as that given to them by the Harter Act of the United States, and which I propose should be given to them under this Bill.
As I stalled at the outset, Mr. Speaker, 1 have no desire to labour the question or to argue it in detail, -but sim-ply to ask the House to accept this explanation and permit me to introduce the Bill. T'heQ I would suggest, if indeed it is open for me to do- so, that thp Bill should be referred to the Select Standing Committee on Railways, Canals -and Telegraph Lines, so that all-parties interested may ha-ve an opportunity to be heard. I- -merely wish to have a fair, frank -and -careful consideration of the question and the principle involved in the Bill which I desire to introduce.

idea is to follow the rules, and that is exactly what I was trying to do. In view of the ruling of the Chair and the advice of the Acting Prime Minister, I will, with the permission of the House, withdraw this
