speakeroldname: Mr. J. H. BURNHAM (West Peterborough) moved:
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, in view of the reported statement by the Reverend Ben Spence, that another Prohibition Referendum in Ontario would cost the prohibitionists five million dollars ($5,000,000), and in view of the fact that such immense sums tend to the corruption by patronage, and otherwise, of press and people arid to the destruction of public liberty and public morals, and in view of the reported collection of party funds for the Farmers' Party and parties, and in view of the fact that a coming struggle in Canada will probably be between the owners of land and the employers of labour and in view of the charges made against other parties in respect of party funds, it is desirable that all campaign funds be prohibited and made a criminal offence and that an amendment of the Criminal Code be made to that effect.
He said. Mr. Speaker, it is altogether top common in matter of this kind, involving general principles such as this does, to meet them, not by argument but by scoffing or some other means of general entertainment, as laughter and sneers, and so to withdraw public attention from their serious nature, in due time this course being treated as a precedent to be followed when some serious business is before the country. It cannot be denied that at the present time there is very serious unrest and discontent in Canada. My charge involved in this resolution is that certain persons are stirring up discontent and apprehension in order to seize power and the advantages accruing therefrom to the detriment of a portion of Canada, chiefly the province of Ontario.
We are not accustomed to arguing things at large in this country or to dealing with them in that general way which is the practice in older countries. People are apt to hurry on without understanding the value of a basic general principle, not knowing, indeed, that a few general principles, especially in statecraft or public conduct, determine the whole principle of government. If they realized that, they would watch the general principles and pay correspondingly little attention to the details. But people are more .carried away in this country by notices they see in the newspapers of some particular details of matters or measures that are before the House or before the country than they are concerned

about the general principles to which these refer or which they trench upon. I assume it will not be denied-that all great movements against the welfare of the State are founded upon corruption and the means of corruption. The chief means of corruption is money, and the value of money in large sums is in the wholesale character of the assault upon the welfare of the State. There can be no objection to. a constituency's managing its own affairs and paying what it likes in the way of expenses of its members. But when that movement becomes national and interests of a wide and national and general character may combine and make assaults upon individual constituencies, it simply means that at some time or another they will gain control of the State for their own ends, all because the principles of a general and national campaign fund has been observed and has not been attacked. It is easy in that way, and it has been easy in the past, for those who have had designs upon the country to make their way. It only remains, as my hon. friend on my right did yesterday, to tsay that everybody knows, every member knows, that funds are spent illegitimately in constituencies, even without the candidate's knowledge. That, of course, I repudiated yesterday in rising to a point of order. But it involves the honour of every man in the House, and if it is true it shows a rottenness and corruption of mind in the average candidate which is beyond belief. It shows that he has a gateway through which this corruption to which I have referred may pass with ease into the general pockets of the country, with ruin to the country and to the people.
It is useless for any part of the population to set itself up above any other part and say, as was well pointed out by the member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) yesterday, et we are holier than thou.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member is not in order in referring to a previous debate during this session. I hope also that he will not go so far as to cover ground which has already been covered this session; his resolution trenches upon a subject which has already been before the House.

I withdraw the remark with reference to a speech made during this session, Mr. Speaker. I simply say that no one part of the population should use language such as " we are holier than thou" to any other part of the population. To presume that two great parties
in this country and all the people who belong to those two great parties are corrupt and willingly corrupt while a new party which has just arisen has come forward for the express purpose of doing away with corruption by the very same means with which they charge the other people with having incurred and enacted corruption, is something that only a very simple people and a very simple party would attempt or allow. The presumption that the old parties have in the past done things with the aid of money in a large fund which they should not have done applies equally to this new party. For them and others to say that a campaign fund is wrong and productive of great harm in one case but all right in the other is to beg the question and to show that they are more inclined to proceed by a policy of bluff than by one of reason and common sense. I myself think, as has been demonstrated historically in the past, that a great national fund is an impropriety. It is a wrong thing; it is unnecessary; it is a source of corruption and danger to the country. As I remarked a few minutes ago, there is no objection to the people of a constituency paying the expenses of their own member. But there is the very greatest possible objection, Mr. Speaker, to a nation-wide campaign fund. That is what I am objecting to; it is dangerous in the extreme.
, We have only to remember what happened in the reign of Queen Elizabeth. At that time, when Spain had determined to conquer England; when Spain had stirred up in the kingdom of Scotland great discontent; when Mary Queen of Scots was a prisoner in England and appealing for the fulfilment of certain rights which she said .she had to the Crown; when the Netherlands were at war with France and with (Spain and were being "assisted directly and indirectly by England; when Ireland was at war with England and had inflicted upon England in the battle of Blackwater the greatest defeat she had ever experienced in Ireland-how was it that the malcontents and those who sought to inspire England gathered themselves together and furthered their cause without incurring the punishment of treason? By means of lampoons; by moans of jokes and all sorts of scoffing and laugh? ter which were apparently intended as jokes, but which really covered up the malicious intent, the malignant intent, the corrupt intent, of those who circulated them. Burleigh, the chief minister of Elizabeth, was not, however, to be bluffed by these

tilings, and he said in some well-known instances that they might be jokes, but they would be provided ^gainst as if they were serious, and I think that advice was good. We know the possibilities of campaign funds, and it is for us as patriotic Canadians to provide against them as if they were serious. We know that few people, who have designs upon the liberties of a country or whose intention it is to possess themselves of the control of that country, would be 'So silly, or stupid, or short-sighted as to proceed directly to the object that they have in view. They would begin by a flank or indirect movement, as we see at the present time some of these flank and indirect movements producing in the minds of the people the first idea which they were intended to produce, namely, apprehension and discontent. I will proceed to illustrate how one of these movements is brought about. You are well aware, Sir, that if men have to withstand grave movements which they plainly see and have set themselves against and have prepared themselves in their own defence against, they will acquit themselves much better, much more amiably and consistently than they would if they were disturbed by some sudden pin-prick of which they had no notice or which they did not understand, but which had suddenly roused them to wrath and antagonism. That is just the artifice that has been adopted in Canada today, and we had an example of it here this last week. Miles Vokes, president of the Dominion Alliance, stated hat the policy of the Dominion Alliance was that it should be its brother's keeper, whether that brother wanted it or not. In other words, they, having made misuse of the voluntary and benevolent idea of sacrificing one's self in order to take care of the moral's good conduct and general benefit of somebody else, having sacrificed themselves to attain a certain end, and they intend to sacrifice the other man and seize power over him and make him do what they wish. That is to say, they are to be their brother's keeper in the sense of having him in jail, and once the people recognizes the fact that it is open to a party or a portion of the people to come forward and say:	You have a right to be your
brother's keeper, and if he does not want you to be his keeper, you have a right to make him; that, of course, is slavery. That is the principle which this man and the Dominion Alliance have laid down. They are determined to seize power and to exercise their power, and they are just as treasonable in their intentions as any other body which wishes to overturn the constitution, 
the general principle of Government, the general principles that safeguard the freedom and liberties of the people. It is idle to say that majorities rule.. The majority rules only just so long as it can rule, because where you have a large compaign fund, and an insidious minority and a designing leader and a so-called alliance, by means of false representations, misrepresentations, dangling before the public things that are not so, you can bedevil the situation and make the people believe anything. As a consequence, it is just like acting in a bargain, disingenuously, dishonestly and unfairly. These people say: We want these things; we have decided to have them; and they proceed by means of any method they can possibly conjure up. The honesty of the thing never appeals to them; they know nothing and they care nothing about that. A common dogfight, or a fight in the bear-pit, or a prizefight is a model of fair *play and virtue alongside the acts which these people will permit themselves to do and which they will do in order to gain their purposes, because they piously and sublimely smile and say that it is for the general benefit, without any regard to whether the other people want it or not. It becomes so far from the general benefit that it turns out to be chiefly for the benefit of the promoters; and when people having enormous campaign funds at the back of their efforts, it is the campaign fund and not the liberty and well-being of the people that they have chiefly in view.
The Rev. Ben Spence has announced that $5,000,000 will be the probable cost of a referendum in Ontario. $5,000,000 means over $60,000 for each constituency, and the man who says to the people of this country that the expenditure of that moneyJs to be legitimate, is telling what he knows to be a lie. A large portion of this money is to be distributed-and nobody c.ould convince me to the contrary-for the benefit of the distributors. $60,000 for each constituency. There never was a campaign fund in Canada that amounted to one-fifth of that for the whole of the Dominion. Yet these same pious frauds will tell us that all that has gone before has been covered with corruption ; they alone are the true, the really good and the beautiful, and they have the impudence to say: Since we know we are so and we are well provided with money, we will put it all over you and put you under our feet and make you do as we please. Therefore, I say that a great campaign fund such as this is against the good morals and the liberty of the people of this country, and I am well advised in saying so.

It is a well-known fact that for many years the Y.M.C.A gathered large sums for the purpose of extending its work as a branch of social service, and beginning, as the founder of that society did, by saying that it was for the furtherance of Christian work, it acquired the respect and support of the public at large. But any one who will follow it up will find that in the course of time the religious part sank into abeyance. The young people did not want too much religion, and they would not have it. You "will observe that religious teaching is away down in the list of the attractions of the Y.M.C.A., and anybody who knows much about the Y.M.C.A. would know that the Christian meetings, the Bible classes and prayer meetings, were attended by barely a corporal's guard, while the gymnasium, the basket-ball team and things of that kind were very well patron-' ized. Public lectures were not looked at. It was impossible to get the young men to attend them. They wanted to enjoy themselves, and nobody would blame them much. In course of time the Y.M.C.A extended the social service idea. After having pointed out how detrimental to the welfare of the country billiards and pool were, they adopted billiards and pool in their programme of attractions, and now you can play billiards and pool in the Y.M.C.A. It was pointed out that the Y.M.C.A. did not pay their full portion of the taxes, claiming that they were a religious institution and were therefore exempt. The people behind the Y.M.C.A were mean enough to profit by that exemption.
I prophesied that the time would come when that small, petty meanness of soul would eat into them and destroy them. It has destroyed them, because they found at their convention in Toronto last year that they could not get along "with social service as the chief end of it, and that they would have to found their future and their whole effort on something else than fees, and they then and there resolved and announced that in future the Y.M.C.A and its principles would be founded, not upon -fees, but upon service. In other words, these young men, instead of being brought up to believe that they were an example to all the Test of mankind, to the mass of the people, to the ragtag and bobtail, to the poor who play their little games in the ditches or any place they can find well, these young nabobs, maintained partly and very largely at public expense, and as objects of charity, had to give up those ideas.
The Y.M.C.A.'s, which were created for the money they could squeeze out of the public, ignored the fact that if they had been worth anything at all, and had had any manhood, they would have offered the advantages of their institutions to the poor who were not able to afford to pay for them. But no, their teaching had not been that. They had in their hearts that meanness and canker which would shrivel them up and destroy them, as it- did. Though millions had been collected, though to all intents and purposes the movement was increasing and becoming exceedingly strong, yet at their convention last year they changed the basis of their whole system, because one ounce of merited blame could blow the whole structure to pieces, and it did so.
Then take these pious and pretentious schemes in other directions for the welfare, say, of the farmer. The Farmers' Organization have adopted the rule that nobody who is not a farmer could join their organization, simply to protect their own interests. They do not say: Come along with us and seize the reins of government. No, they unfurl the flag of some benevolent scheme, some meriltricious humbug, and say: Subscribe largely to the great campaign against corruption, and by means of the campaign against corruption they will get into power, and then they will promote their own agricultural interests, and they will tell us all the time that it is for the benefit ot Canada, while at the same time they would not allow any one who is not a farmer .to join them lest some small portion of their effort might be for the general benefit of Canada, and the Farmers' party do not desire that. That is one of the singular things that is presented in this movement a!t the present day, but if anybody wants to get a nice little peep into the action of this kind of people, and see1 how ready they are to destroy the liberties of the people for their own ends, they have only to look at the Ontario Temperance Act, which is now being both promulgated and amended to perfection, and is double copper-bottomed and riveted so that there is no escape. Some benevolent people connected with the movement would even have flogging provided as a penalty, and I think it should be, because 'then some of these people would be the first to he flogged. Let me show the condition of society in the province of Ontario, a portion of ithe Dominion of Canada, by reading to you subsection

(2) of section 61 of the Ontario Temperance Act, Chap. 50, which say,s:
All information or complaints for the prosecution of any offence against any of the provisions of this Act	 may he made
without any oath or affirmation to the truth thereof.
Any mean sneaking informer, or other blackguard, is good enough to bring a complaint against the finest lady or gentleman in the land. * Any one who knows or cares about British liberty would not tolerate any such thing for a moment. While the people of Ontario do not understand it, by a sort of Nemesis Sir William Hearst met his fate and went down to that disgrace which he well deserved. After the case has been brought .to court on the information of somebody who need not say that he was speaking the truth, because ten to one he was not, 'there is no way of getting back at the wretch that gave the impious information. Section 83 provides that.
In proving the sale or disposal, giving, purchasing, or receiving gratuitously or otherwise, or consumption of liquor, for the purpose of any proceeding relative to any offence under this Act, it shall not he necessary to show that any money actually passed, or any liquor was actually consumed, if the magistrate or justice or justices hearing the case is or are satisfied that a transaction in the nature of a sale or other disposal, giving, purchasing or receiving, actually took place or that any consumption of liquor was about to take place.
Theire is no evidence required if the absolute judge on the bench in his serene majesty is satisfied that the party, if not guilty, would be guilty if he had a chance. Not in the whole history, I would not say of jurisprudence, because I do not wish to insult the history of law, but noit in the [whole history of informers from the beginning of the world was there any such contemptible camouflage as that, or such a piece of outrageous bluff. They are doing this in the very face of the people, who think, by reason of their protests and piety, that there is some little honour and decency and justice left in them, when there is not. The day will come when they will be thrown into the garbage can, but in the meantime they can do this country incalculable damage, and it is against that I wish to protest. Bolshevism in the same disregard of. the fundamentals of liberty and order. It is simply making up your mind that you wantsomething and you are going to have it; and as heretofore in the history of the world it has been wise for men to pretend that they were right whether they were or 
not, since there was always something in the moral value and weight of such an assertion, so the Bolshevist pure and simple states that he will bring about what he desires by such means as he may care to use. And while he will make the rivers run with blood, he will point to the few goods things which he will do,-because, after all, it is only a great blackguard who cannot do some few good things. He will point to some of the few good things which he will have brought about, as, for instance, the overthrow of absolutism and autocracy. But he will have to admit, nevertheless, that he did not proceed according to any principle of justice or law except his own sweet will; and we have in Bolshevism precisely what we have in the actions of the Dominion Alliance, without any difference whatever. I say that they are creating in the minds of the people of the country an indifference to utterly irregular proceedings and principles, and when the people become accustomed-to disregard the fundamentals of law and justice and the ancient practice of these principles, they will throw them to one side; and from having become temperance fanatics, they will bloom forth as full-fledged Bolshevists, because they will have learned their lesson. They will have learned that it is not necessary to regard the present liberties of the people, or to consider the liberties that have been
Tu n	past- Their attitude will be
this: \\hat we want is right; we-must have it, and we will have it;" and they will proceed to get it by great campaign funds or other means of corruption and by force Ihey will argue that the end justifies the means, especially if the end be what they want. This is the principle which will be inculcated and drilled into the minds of the people. At the present time the great complaint of the farming community is that labour is too expensive, and that it is so high that the cost of production has made farming a non-paying industry.
Mr. CALDWELL; We are objecting to farm machinery costing so much on account of the duty there is on it.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that he is satisfied with the price of labour?
Yes, and I hire labour myself.
Is the whole farming movement satisfied?	'

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
I am speaking only for myself.

I can tell the hon. gentleman that unless the farming community, that is to say, the Farmers' party, have gone back on their platform and their principles-which, of course, is possible they have said time and time again, and Hansard frequently records the assertion, that the cost of production, owing to the price of labour, is so high that they cannot make farming pay, and that the great increase in wages has acted as one of the most serious drawbacks to the prosecution of agriculture. No one will deny that they [DOT] have made this statement. The directors of labour, and labour itself throughout the country, say very truly that the cost of consumption is so great that labourers must have their wages increased from time to time, and they allege that in many cases they are near to the bread line. They say that it is imperative that the people of the country should seriously consider their circumstances, because as a rule it is assumed that labour works 313 days in the year, which it does not and cannot in this country; that is, not.considering the mechanical part of labour alone but the labouring element. The mass of every day outdoor workingmen have an extremely hard time of it owing to the weather, and consequently they are nearer to the bread line than any other class of people. The day will come when the farmer who holds the land and now seeks to get legal and governmental control of the country will be the only person that will be opposed to the man who wants higher wages. And since the farmer's cry is that higher wages is the chief source of his complaint, while the labourer finds, in the high cost of farm produce and the food he has to buy, the principal element of his hardships, you will have the farmer or the owner of the land at daggers drawn with the labourer and the employer of labour; and when men realize that they may say to themselves: "Stand not upon the order of your going, but go and get what you want, for you can have as big a corruption fund as you like, and disregard all the old and time-honoured principles of moral conduct and religion." When we [DOT]have reached this pass, Mr. Speaker, then I say we shall have paved the way to civil war. And without being the slightest bit apprehensive of exciting ridicule !I tell you solemnly that in this country, indeed, on this continent, just for the very reasons I have indicated, especially by reason of the
turmoil and discontent stirred up by those people who want great campaign funds, and who zealously disregard the liberties of the people, we are more than likely to have civil strife. Under these chaotic circumstances people do not appeal to elections; they do not appeal to governments; ^ they do not appeal to public opinion. How can they appeal to public opinion when that opinion has discarded all regard for the principles of justice, and when every man feels that he can get no consideration? Under these conditions, Sir, the discontented man will say in his heart, "T will get what I want if I have to seize it"; and that is the condition of affairs to which present events are leading up. This disastrous impasse will be brought about and financed by great national campaign funds; it never could take place except by the aid of such funds. And therefore I say that the Liberal and Conservative parties, the Farmers' party, and the people generally will be well advised to heed the signs of the times, to wrest from the Farmers' party and from those who can foment this sort of disturbance the weapons at their disposal, and to withdraw from Ben iSpence and all people of his ilk, who are prepared to undertake the gratuitous keep of their brothers, whether their brothers so desire or not, the power of having vast sums at their command for the purpose of disregarding the principles of justice and liberty, and creating disturbances that must inevitably tend to civil war. For thjs is what their machinations will lead to.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that we should show some of the old fashioned patriotic feeling in this House. The hon. member for As-siniboia (Mr. Gould) admitted yesterday that in 1911 the suspicion was that the country had been flooded by a great national corruption fund. All you have to do is to get the idea the corruption funds are afloat and you have the public shivering and trembling and believing that they are about to be bribed. You have given them the high cost of living, you have put them in the bread line and then you offer them a large corruption fund. Everything that will possibly develop such a condition is in this country and if those who are fairly well versed in the history of the British Empire to cast their eye over this history, what do they see? The same conditions arising in Canada that arose, and produced ' such disastrous results before. Mankind is very much the same all over. It does not do to trust anybody. If, during the

course of a long life they succeed in behaving themselves no doubt they will pass on to their reward but it is well for us not to give credit to professions when a farmer makes the claim that he is entitled to a great campaign fund. When he says that in his hands it is a campaign fund and that in our hands it is a corruption fund what he states is false and must be regarded with suspicion. A large central organization, whether actuated by a political, a prohibition or any other idea, even if it were sincere, or even if it were densely ignorant and sincere, or even if it might in time succeed in doing some good, might become the victim of designing people who, having seen it built up and erected, might make use of it for their own purposes and would proceed to do so. Remove the weapons and you remove the danger. It is for us to do that and not to listen to any 5 p.m. professions at all. Let every constituency, if it wants to, pay its own expenses.
Thank you.

If that is what the bon. gentleman is thanking me for, I will give him something to thank me for. The country wants no more national corruption funds and we are not going to have them whether they may be for the Liberal party, the Conservative party or the Farmers' party. And we are not going to have any fancy statements that are not in conformity with the law at all. Behind some of these statements there may lurk a great deal but from what we see in front of them it is not worth while to go behind them. There is nothing about them that is extremely attractive, or pretty. The people of this country are well aware of what the condition of affairs is but they are a confiding people. They are apt to think sometimes, especially when they are disquieted and harassed by high taxes that they had better shake themselves together and bring about a change. It may be so but this is the time of danger. Looking to those who are courting your approval it is well to see that their professions are not too great because my opinion is that the more piety a man professes the more dangerous he is, that the real saint is the man who is discovered by means of his goodness, not by means of his pretensions. The man who is too good feels that if he does not take hold of humanity by the neck and shake it until it is put into proper condition, the universe will be shaken to its foundations and that God who gave us liberty will find out the
	,,
mistake He has made from the professions of the prohibitionists and perhaps the farmers.

Mr. Speaker, I have seconded this resolution of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Burnham) more for the purpose of allowing him to get the resolution before the House than for anything else. While I do agree with a considerable amount that the hon. gentleman has said, I do not agree with all the sentiments expressed in his speech. I think there are campaign funds and campaign funds. Where a campaign fund is used for political or other corruption of any kind it becomes a menace to the public. But a campaign fund, in my opinion, is necessary to some extent in every great movement provided it is used legitimately. To that extent I do believe that it is necessary to have a campaign fund. Where a campaign fund, such as the hon. gentleman has mentioned in connection with the prohibition movement in Ontario, of something like $5,000,000, is used to influence people to vote for anything that they do not believe in, it becomes a corrupting influence. I do say that this is an immense campaign fund and I do not think it could be used legitimately for the purpose for which it might be raised. We know that in connection with the forward movement of the churches the great fund which has been collected is one which would not be used for corrupting influences. Therefore, we cannot say that every campaign fund would be used for such a purpose. Campaign funds are all necessary in political campaigns, I do not wish to discuss the resolution but I only wished to put myself on record in regard to the matter with which it deals.
Mr. THOMAS W. CALDWELL (Victoria and Carleton, N.B.): Mr. Speaker, I wish to offer -a few remarks in regard to this resolution. I was very much pleased to hear the hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) declare at the outset that he had no objection to the electors in any constituency paying the expenses of their candidate in an election campaign. As far as I am aware this is the only thing that has been done by the New Progressive Party up to the present time, and as far as I know it is the only thing that is proposed to be done.
But, Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend's remarks are not very consistent with his resolution, because there he states that all campaign funds be prohibited. Now, if he

will make his resolution read, "that all campaign funds, except for legitimate election expenses, be prohibited," I will hold up both hands in hearty support, because that is what I believe in and I think that is what every member of the Progressive Party believes in,-that there shall not be one dollar of our campaign funds used for anything but illegitimate purposes.
Oh, oh.

Well, Mr. Speaker, 1 am glad to see hon. members are able to get a little comfort out of a slip of the tongue. An Irishman is allowed to speak once and explain himself afterwards-there is a certain amount of Irish in me; also a little Scotch,-although it is not distilled Scotch. I meant of course to use the words "legitimate purposes."
Another remark my hon. friend made was that you can make the people believe anything. I assume he believes that or he would not have made some of the statements he uttered this afternoon. A certain circus man has said: You can fool all the people part of the time, and part of the people all the time. But I would warn the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) that he cannot fool all the people all the time.

It is a circus surely
that he would quote from.

: Referring to the hon. member's statement that he is willing to allow constituents to pay their candidate's legitimate expenses, I would like to refer briefly to my own election. At the time I was nominated I absolutely refused to accept the nomination because I am a very busy man. Perhaps my time is not as valuable as -that of the hon. member for West Peterborough, but I felt I would have to make a very great sacrifice indeed to accept nomination even to a seat in this House. However, when our convention- and I want to tell the House that it was thoroughly representative of the two counties composing my constituency, and they are not two of the least counties in the province of New Brunswick;, and that province, although of small area, is not one of the most unimportant of the provinces- when that convention insisted on my accepting the nomination, I decided that it was my duty to do so, but I told them that I must impose the terms on which I shall accept it. The terms were that the electors should pay my legitimate campaign expenses, that they must not spend one dollar for anything but legitimate expenses, and
that after the election they must have those accounts audited and published, and if I found they had spent one dollar for illegitimate purposes I would resign my seat. Because, Mr. Speaker, I would disdain to occupy a seat in this House if it cost one dollar to buy a vote to elect me. While I consider it the highest honour that can be conferred upon men to elect them as representatives of the people in this House, I think the, man who buys his way into Parliament is condemned before he comes here.
Then, Mr. Speaker, we have been accused of being elected by the United Farmers. I want to tell the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Burnham)-and perhaps he is not to blame for some of these statements; possibly we may attribute part of them to his ignorance of conditions and of the size of the farmers' movement in the East-but I want to tell him and other hon. members that the farmers' movement is very small indeed in New Brunswick. For instance, Igot 1,000 more votes in the counties I represent than there were United Farmers in the whole province. And during the campaign I never personally asked one elector to vote for me. I spoke at several of our farmers' clubs, and I can prove this statement, that I told them upon every occasion I did not want them to feel under any obligation to vote for me simply because they belonged to the United Farmers' Organization and I happened to be their President. I told them, " If you do not want to elect an independent man as your member, do not vote for me, because I will guarantee to be strictly independent if elected, and I will use my best judgment as to what course to take on any matters that may come before the House of Commons."
I do not wish to take up the time of the House at any great length, Mr. Speaker, but I would like to say that I was somewhat surprised to find a man who presumably bv the wording of his resolution is a self-confessed uplifter, so strongly opposed to prohibition. I want to tell him that I am in favour of prohibition, and that the mud he slung at the prohibitionists comes from him with a very bad grace indeed. He stated that he believed the Farmers' party would be thrown into the garbage barrel. Mr. Speaker, I hope when that happens the people will take my hon. friend out of the barrel before they put me in, for I would not like to occupy the same barrel with him.
Another statement that somewhat surprised me, coming from such an eminent uplifter, was that he would admit that even

he could be unseated for corrupt practices at his election.
I did not say that.
Mr. Speaker, I appeal to the House that I am right. He said that he did not believe-

I bow to your ruling, Mr. Speaker. If I misquote my hon. friend I want him -to correct me. He said that he did not believe there was a member of this House who could not be unseated if the matter was followed up.

I said with reference to the statement yesterday of the hon. member for Assimboia (Mr. Gould) that I did not believe there was a member in this House who, if be put in such a statement, could not be unseated.
Mr. -CALDWELL:	Pardon me, Mr. Speaker, evidently I misunderstood my hon. friend. If he had made the statement which I understood him to- make, I would like to take issue with him. I defy any man to unseat me, because I am thoroughly convinced that my supporters carried out the instructions I gave them when I accepted their nomination. If I were not well convinced of that fact I would not occupy my seat in this House five minutes longer.

Mr. Speaker, before the motion is adopted I would like to give the House a little information and show the "line-up," if I may use the phrase, in which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Burnham) is evidently -placing us by his attitude on different questions. I have before me a -copy of Toronto Saturday Night of April 10, 1920, headed "The New Salvation, by J. H. Burnham, M.A., M.P."-the gentleman who introduced this resolution. I just wish to quote a few of his statements ,so that the people throughout the Dominion will be able to place a proper value on what he has said in regard to the prohibition movement and also in regard to the new political movement which he gives the agriculturalists credit for propagating.
Read it all.

It is a rather lengthy article and I will merely give a few quotations to sho-w the attitude of the writer on certain matters. He says:

It matters not that individual liberty is tied in chains. Do as you are told-it is not for the individual to work out his own salvation. The majority decides all and for all. The policeman and the informer do the rest.
Further on I find this statement:
The drama of life, in which the individual stands before God in the full glare of sin and temptation and leaning on Christ, conquers evt n death itself, and in triumph enters into rest- is a play that is played out.
Now, if that is not a most significant statement coming from a gentleman who undertakes in this case to castigate those who are' trying to bring about better conditions

I may explain that
that is a sarcastic reference to statements made by prohibitionists. They say that the drama is played out and that they have introduced something new.
That is the hon. member's interpretation of what they say, not their statement.
Be fair about it.

Then he says:
The death of Jesus Christ was a mistake Ii was a fearful error. If God had not made it easy to sin and prohibited the means of evil there would have been no fall, and man would pursue his way in life like the eagle or the song bird, unmindful of that which he could no longer turn to his own destruction, sinless and shameless.
Now, I just mention these few things to let the public know the calibre of the hon. gentleman and the ideas upon which he evidently bases his argument. He says further :
Had the Deity been " a man " of efficient actio

, and a member of the W.C.T.U.. he would have slain the serpent ere he created it. and would have destroyed the vine that made Noah drunk.	/
He undertakes in this issue of Saturady Night to criticize the Deity; then he comes here to-day and criticizes the Rev. Ben Spence, the Woman's Christian Temperance Union, and prohibition in general. He winds up by giving members of the cross benches a little advice. He is welcome to give all the advice that he wishes; the more unfounded ridicule he offers to us the better we shall be satisfied.
Then, in Ms article he goes on to say- and this is the most striking evidence of his attitude:
" I am the Vine." said Christ. " Cursed be the Vine." say we.
The only inference from this remark is that when Christ said "I am the Vine,"

he was referring to the vine that produces the wine that sparkles, and so on. There are several other similar statements in the article, but I shall not go into them further. I have given sufficient, I think, to let the people of Canada understand the calibre of the hon. gentleman and the ideals that he upholds.
Now, let us turn back to his resolution. He wants to make it a criminal offence for any one to make contributions of any kind to campaign funds; yet be states today that he has absolutely no objection to constituencies providing their own funds to carry on their own election campaigns. I want to inform the hon. member that that is exactly what the farmers of Western Canada are doing. Every constituency controls their own fund; it is 'in their own hands; they collect it and they control it. Where, then, is this tremendous fund that the hon. member speaks of, and which is to be used to corrupt all and sundry? Nothing was said about the back-door method, the underhand or secret method that nobody knew anything kbout, until the honest and aboveboard method was practised. The underhand method has been going on and on and nobdy has made objection to it, but now that the light has been thrown upon it and proper methods adopted of collecting campaign funds, methods that will do away with corruption, our uplifters, if we may use the term employed by our friend from New Brunswick (Mr. Caldwell) take objection.
My hon. Mend goes back to the reign of Queen Elizabeth. That is another indication of just how up-to-date he is. He would be well-advised to move forward a step or two and try to get himself up to modern times when he undertakes to criticise popular movements that are taking place today.
I do not intend to make any defence as against my hon. friend's argument or to refute further the assertions which he has made. But his attitude on this question reminds me of a story which I heard a little while ago of two gentlemen from the Emerald Isle who had just come to this country. They thought that they would go on a little hunting expedition, and not being familiar with our game they were not very successful. They were returning home when they 'happened to hear something knocking, and on looking up they saw a woodpecker hammering away on the side of a tree. Pat, who was carrying the gun, was getting ready to pot the bird, not knowing just what it was, but Mike, who was
more observant cried out: "Hold on, Pat, just laive him alone; he'll batter his uwn brains out."

The hon. gentleman has paid me the compliment of alleging that I have some brains, a compliment which I am sorry I cannot pay him in turn. I wish to say-
Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER* Unless the hon. member is rising for the purpose of making some explanation of the citation made by the member for Maple Creek (Mr. Maharg)-
I was closing.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is my duty to remind the House that the member for West Peterborough is about to close the debate, and that if any other hon. member wishes to speak he should do so now.

Mr. Speaker, because I am on the same side of the House as the hon. member who has introduced this resolution (Mr. Burnham) I do not wish it to be understood that I endorse in the slightest degree the position that he has taken this afternoon. I am decidedly opposed to it, as well as to the spirit in which he expressed his views and to very much of the language by means of which he expressed them.
I do not intend to discuss the name that is mentioned in the resolution. Hon. members from Ontario will be in a position to give proper weight to any remarks which have been made respecting the gentleman concerned. However, in passing I may say that my experience has been that in the main those who are opposed to the principle of prohibition have been far more ready to produce large campaign funds to support the continuance of the liquor traffic than temperance people have been able to do in their idea of promoting the principle of prohibition and total abstinence.
It is useless at this time to take any position opposed to prohibition. I speak not simply of prohibition of the liquor traffic, but of prohibition as a principle, as a policy. The fact of the matter, Sir, is this: unless we admit the principle and policy of prohibition, civilization becomes chaos. All legislation is based upon the principle of prohibition; if there are no prohibitions there is no civilization. Civilization rests upon certain recognized principles, one of which is that certain things must be prohibited. I do not intend to develop the argument in regard to the liquor question; that is not necessary on this occasion. But
I

I wish to say that I am an agrarian, though not a member of the Agrarian party. But if I were a member of the Agrarian party, I should consider myself in very good company, whereas I am lost in the company of the hon. member who has virtually denounced the prohibitionists, the Y.M.C.A. workers, the W.C.T.U. leaders, and the members of the Agrarian party. On the whole, it is not a bad quartette. I want to state here openly and candidly that I do not endorse the position taken by my hon. friend (Mr. Burnham) although I am on the same side of the House as the hon. gentleman. I do not believe in his principle, nor in his policy, nor in his spirit, nor in the attitude taken towards the great movements which have brought society up to the high position that it occupies to-day in regard to the moral questions to which he has indirectly referred and which, in the main, I am sorry to say he has appeared to denounce or, at any rate, to ridicule. I regret that such a position was taken to-day in this House, and I want to place myself on record as being opposed to such a position and as being stiongly in support of the principles which these bodies have so long and faithfully enunciated and maintained before the people, namely, the prohibition of the liquor traffic in this country as a business, and also the ideals, social, economic, moral and religious, which the Y.M.C.A. and the W.C.T.U. have, to the extent of their ability, set before the people of Canada as being worthy of their adoption and achievement.
Mr. JOHN F. REIID (Mackenzie): Mr. Speaker, I wish to say just a few words in reference to the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Peterborough West (.Mr. Burnham). The resolution says in part:
And in view of the fact that such immense sums-*
Referring to this $5,000,000 campaign fund to be collected by the prohibitionists.
-tend_ to the corruption by patronage, and otherwise, of press and people and to the destruction of public liberty and public morals.
Then the hon. member has a crack at the Farmers' party.
And in view of the reported collection of party funds for the Farmers' party and parties.
He should have inserted here "and funds from the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, or what is known to-day as the Reconstruction Association."
All parties are referred to.

I have not the least doubt that the hon. member knows whereof he speaks in regard to corruption from patronage and from campaign funds which from some unknown source have come to his constituency and to every other constituency in this Dominion. He has now a nightmare; he sees the Farmers' party rising, and in his feeble endeavour he is trying to do his little bit to put the Farmers' party out of business. We welcome such attempts as he has put forward; that is powder to us; it gives us more strength.
My hon. friend used very strong language in regard to what would be the eventual effect on the country of the Farmers' party going from door to door soliciting campaign funds. He went even so far as to suggest treason and, if I forget not, civil war. I should like my hon. friend, when he replies in closing the debate, to explain to the House just what he means by treason, and, perhaps, civil war, and how the actions of this new movement are going to bring about this terrible calamity which he sees, probably, in his slumbers. He says further that we have the impudence to dare to collect funds, flf am of the opinion, and I believe that it is the opinion held by all ~ those who see this movement as this Farmers' group sees it, that the cause of this movement was the unlimited supply of slush funds that came into our constituents in the West to debauch the electorate.
I challenge my hon. friend to contradict that.
I did not catch what the hon. gentleman said. A page who happened to speak to me interrupted me.

One of the causes of the rise of this new movement in the Farmers' Organizations in collecting in their constituencies their campaign funds was the fact that under the old party system thousands of dollars were brought into each constituency,-I am speaking more particularly of the West, about which I know -to debauch the electorate.

I have no doubt
about that.
Mr. J. F, REID: The hon. member knows all about it.
I do not know all about it.

The first election campaign I saw in the Dominion of Canada was

in 1882, and I have been more or less active in election campaigns from that time until now. I have seen some of the workings of this mysteriously received campaign fund. We knew not whence it came, but we had an idea. It is the wish of the (fanners' movement to put a stoip 'to all that; that there should be no more of it, and I think every hon. gentleman in this House will hail the day when that is put a stop to. If each constituency would take upon itself the responsibility of financing its own candidate, then there would be no opportunity for the big concerns to dump in the'ir slush funds.	>
May I ask my hon. friend a question?
Yes, ask all you like.

Is it not a fact that one of the promoters of the original organization of the United Farmers of Ontario made the statement that it was the money that was supplied to them by the Grain Growers of the West and the assistance and advice they received from the leader of the party over there that they were enabled to carry on at the outset? Will he deny that the money was supplied by the Grain Growers of the West?
Will my hon. friend make his question a little clearer? I am rather slow to catch on. Has he reference to political funds?
Most assuredly.
Then I say: No, not one dollar of political funds went from the West to the United Farmers of Ontario.

But they are a political organization, and one of the original members of that party published a statement in which.he says that had it not been for the money received from the Grain Growers of the West, they would not have been able to carry on.
Carry on what?
The organization of the United Farmers of Ontario.
That is different altogether. I am speaking of political organizations; my hon. friend is speaking of Grain Growers' Association^.
They are all political organizations.	,

The hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Burnham) stated 79
that labour was complaining of the high cost of living and that the farmers were complaining of the high price of labour. Speaking as a farmer, I am perfectly satisfied to pay labour the wage which it asks for, and I will ask the hon. member to join with the Farmers' Organization and help out labour and help us to take the duty off foodstuffs so that labour may have food cheaper, thus reducing the cost of living.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) :
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise not to take part in the discussion which has covered a fairly wide field of opinion upon many questions which were, perhaps, not absolutely essential to the proper determination whether we ought to make the creation of any campaign fund a criminal offence. I rise simply to suggest to the hon. member who introduced the resolution that he might, perhaps, consider whether he might not with propriety withdraw that resolution. He has had an opportunity of very fully and frankly exposing his views on the different matters that are referred to in the motion.
He has evoked what may be described as a very frank and a very full expression of views on these different questions not quite in accord with his own. So far as the purpose he seeks to achieve by this motion is concerned, I should like to call his attention to the fact that we have presently before the House a^ franchise Bill dealing with questions precisely of this kind, and I would suggest to him that that perhaps would be the proper place for the House to arrive at a conclusion with regard to the desirability of making provision concerning campaign funds in general and campaign funds of particular kinds. Having that opportunity, 1 would suggest to the hon. gentleman that he would Jose nothing by withdrawing the present motion, if he desires to insist upon his proposal that funds of that nature should be absolutely prohibited as being criminal offences. In this connection perhaps I might take the liberty of suggesting, to him, as his resolution is apparently based on a report as to a very large sum of money which a reverend gentleman has estimated as being necessary to carry on a particular campaign for prohibition, that the report, as Mark Twain said of the report of his death, may be somewhat exaggerated. It seems a trifle difficult to believe that the reverend gentleman referred to, the Rev. Mr. Spence, who from his general record we all I am sure, are satisfied is, generally speaking, most temperate in his habits, could have contracted such very ex-



pensive habits with regard to campaign j funds. Perhaps with that as an additional reason, the hon. gentleman might be satisfied to withdraw his resolution with a view, perhaps, to satisfying himself more perfectly as to the accuracy of the report upon which he premises his conclusions.
Mr. JOHN H. BURNHAM: Mr. Speaker, when I put this resolution on the Order Paper the Franchise Act, so far as I knew, was not then in contemplation. I quite agree that the clause in the Franchise Act which has been adopted referring to campaign funds probably covers the dangerous phase to which I refer in my resolution.
I wish to say in regard to farmers that I had no intention of condemning farmers or even the Farmers' party, but I did condemn many of the principles which they laid down in their platform, among them being what I understood to be a national campaign fund.
It is a national campaign fund that I object to, and not constituency campaign funds. Perhaps my resolution might be plainer in that respect.
As to my reference to treason, which an hon. member asked me to explain, I did not refer to the Farmers' party in particular, but to all movements which might have a sinister bearing on the policy of the country. Like Caesar's wife they must avoid the very suspicion of evil, and if they do not, they must be prevented from doing evil. We must observe the principle - that all men are equal before the law.
With regard to prohibition, the reason why I ridicule and fight it is because it is an anti-Christian measure. No man can be a prohibitionist without sneering at the policy of the Most High, "which is not prohibition. There is no prohibition of evil in the Christian religion. The prohibitionist cannot be a religious man; he is nothing but a tyrant. It is because I hope that 1 am at heart a Christian and a religious man that I am fighting prohibition, and will fight it to the end, because I believe that it does not come from God, and it cannot be supported by a single quotation from the Word of God. I believe it comes from the devil, whither it will go. I withdraw the resolution.
Resolution withdrawn.
On the Orders of the Day:

I prer *sume that the Government will be agree-

*able to bringing down the correspondence between the Grand Trunk Railway Company and the Government, with respect to the agreement that Parliament is to be asked to confirm. I think the correspondence will be necessary if we are to discuss intelligently the agreement before confirming it.
It will be brought down. We might call it six o'clock, I think.
What business does 'the Government intend to take up tomorrow?

The Grand
Trunk Bill, and as soon as that is finished we will take up the Franchise Bill.
I think we should have the correspondence before we discuss the Bill.
Does my hon. friend object to going on with the Bill to-morrow?

It is a Bill of only two clauses, I understand. One *clause is to correct an error. We could take that, but I do not think we should be asked to confirm the agreement until we have the correspondence.

We will tackle the Bill and see what progress we can make.
